newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition stays on protest course.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition stays on protest course.

text.p: Serbian opposition parties vowed on Saturday to maintain pressure on President Slobodan Milosevic ahead of a Sunday deadline for courts to rule on whether the ruling Socialists cheated them of election victory.

Thousands of their supporters have braved rain, cold and fear of the police for the past five days across Serbia, demanding the authorities reverse their decision to annul local election results which would have awarded the opposition victory in most of the biggest Serbian towns.
Courts have to pass judgement on those annulments by Sunday evening.
Opposition leaders said they were preparing to expand the protests if the courts failed to uphold their victory.
"We hope that the judges are aware of their responsiblities," Zoran Djindjic, leader of the Democratic party, told Reuters.
Student leaders said they were preparing sit-ins on Monday at Belgrade faculties and trade unions were considering launching strikes.
Opposition officials say international support could make the difference between success and failure for the opposition.
"What would help would be to employ the already proven method in which (U.S. President Bill) Clinton or (French President Jacques) Chirac telephones Milosevic," Djindjic said.
International pressure helped force the former communist leader to ditch nationalist war aims and agree a peace settlement forged in Dayton a year ago.
Western powers were slow to react to the opposition charges but after several days of protests the United States and Britain have voiced grave concerns about possible fraud.

Privately many opposition leaders fear the Western powers are reluctant to intervene for fear of alienating Milosevic, a pivotal figure in the Balkans who forced the Bosnian Serbs to accept the Dayton accords and made peace with Bosnia and Croatia.
Milosevic himself has not commented on the annulments but state media has delivered mixed signals and an allied party condemned them in clear terms.

State television broadcast a statement on Thursday from Nova Democratija (New Democracy), a member of Milosevic's leftist coalition, which denounced election rigging and called for the will of the people to be respected.
Its headquarters were bombed hours later.
